p: The Manas, known in Bhutan as the Drangme Chhu, is the largest of Bhutan's four major river systems. It drains 41,350 square kilometres of eastern Bhutan and northeast India through three main branches, the Drangme Chhu, the Mangde Chhu and the Bumthang or Chamkhar Chhu. Part of its main stem rises in southern Tibet at about 4,500 metres and enters India in the Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh before crossing into Bhutan near Trashigang. The Lhobrak or Kuri Chhu, its main central tributary, is the only one that rises north of the Great Himalayas.

In Bhutan the river runs southwest through V-shaped gorges between two ranges of the Lower Himalayas. In the foothills the valley widens into swamps and marshes. The Aie River joins it in Assam, and it then meanders for about 75 kilometres to the Brahmaputra near Jogighopa. It is the largest tributary on the Brahmaputra's north bank and contributes 5.48 per cent of its average volume. From May to October the southwest monsoon brings more than 4,000 millimetres of rain to the southern part of the basin; the flow in the monsoon is said to be as much as 20 times that of the dry season.

The core of the present Manas Wildlife Sanctuary in Assam was designated a sanctuary in 1928 and declared a tiger reserve in 1978; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in December 1985. A dam proposed in the 1970s would have sent a canal 100 kilometres long through the tiger reserve to the Sankosh River. India's Ministry of Environment and Forests objected, the World Heritage Committee of UNESCO supported the objection, and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi discontinued the project. Two dams proposed on the Bhutanese side were dropped in 1986. In February 1989 members of the All Bodo Students Union entered the park and killed several wardens and guards.

The lowlands north of the confluence, the Duars, are very fertile and have been made into tea estates and paddy fields. Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan, raised to a national park in 1993, is 92 per cent forested, and five thousand people live in villages inside it. The two reserves shelter the Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, greater one-horned rhinoceros, wild water buffalo, pygmy hog, hispid hare and golden langur, and the Ganges river dolphin lives in the river.

notes: The article contradicts itself on figures, so I left them out: total length 400 km in the lede but 376 km in Geography; Royal Manas National Park 43,854 ha (established 1966) in the lede but 9,938.54 km2 in its own section, where the same figure is also given for both reserves together; the Indian sanctuary 'established at 391,000 ha in 1955 and increased to 95,000 ha'; '30 mm of annual rainfall' in the sanctuary.
The article says the Bodoland agitation centred on the park 'in 1980'; I used only the dated February 1989 event.
No pre-20th-century history is in the article (the Ahom frontier of the existing description is not mentioned there).
